newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RUGBY UNION-ARU DEFENDS DECISION TO PLAY IN MELBOURNE.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-ARU DEFENDS DECISION TO PLAY IN MELBOURNE.

text.p: Australian rugby union officials have defended their decision to play their annual showpiece match in Melbourne, heartland of Australian Rules football, instead of the traditional sites of Sydney or Brisbane.
The Australian Rugby Union (ARU) say holding next Saturday's Bledisloe Cup match at the Melbourne Cricket Ground (MCG), a decision which has outraged traditionalists, would be good for the game.

"The Bledisloe Cup is the most important game on the Australian rugby calendar and the MCG is the biggest stadium in the country so it makes sense to bring the two together," ARU general manager Matt Carroll said.
"It is an exciting time for rugby and this is a major part of the game's development."
Opponents of the move say it is tantamount to treason to take the game away from its grassroots supporters in the northern states of New South Wales and Queensland.
Fans who had supported the game for years in its previous amateur guise had felt betrayed by the move to professionalism and considered the move to Melbourne, announced last year, the final straw.

But the ARU said thousands of rugby followers would have been denied the chance of attending the match if it had been played in Sydney and Brisbane and going south was a way of making the game more accessible.
The MCG has seating for 100,000, compared to the Sydney Football Stadium's capacity of 40,000, of which only 6,000 seats are made available to the general public.
Tickets for Saturday's match were sold out within a day, ensuring that the day will see the biggest crowd ever to attend a rugby match in Australia.

Carroll said international matches played in Sydney or Brisbane usually generated about one million Australian dollars ($737,000) in gate receipts, with the current record standing at $A1.6 million for last year's match against world champions South Africa in Sydney.
He said the Melbourne match was expected to be worth about $A4 million.
"In financial terms, taking the game to Melbourne is a good move but this is not just about money," Carroll said. "This is about taking the game to the whole country.
"It wouldn't have mattered if only 55,000 people had turned up. We wanted to spread the game."
Carroll said the most pleasing aspect of taking the match to Melbourne was that the majority of tickets were purchased by local people, belying claims that Victorians would not attend the match.
"There's about 15,000 (people) flying over from New Zealand and about 20,000 coming down from New South Wales and Queensland but the rest have been bought by Victorians.
Touts have reportedly been selling tickets for five times their face value, a week before the game.
"Interest in the game has exceeded our expectations," said Carroll, adding that it was unlikely to be a one-off.
"We are aware that not everyone is happy with our decision to take the game there but the numbers speak for themselves and we can say with confidence that the game will be a great success.
"I think there's also every chance that Melbourne may get to host a match every year from now." ($ = 1.355 Australian Dollars)
